The vivid recollection of that day would surface unexpectedly, and Amina would feel as if the threat had returned, her heart racing as if she were back in the combat zone, amplifying her sense of danger. The traumatic memories of that incident haunted her relentlessly, particularly the sounds of explosions that echoed in her mind every time she heard a loud bang. The sound of an explosion would pull her back into the chaos of that day, flooding her mind with vivid memories and leaving her disoriented and afraid, as if the danger were still all around her. Whenever she heard those sounds, they would pull the vivid memories of the ambush into sharp focus, making her feel as if she were reliving the chaos, amplifying her anxiety and sense of danger. Even the faintest whiff of cologne in her office would send her spiraling back to those moments of horror, making her feel trapped in a cycle of fear. In those moments, Amina would stop taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again, convinced that avoidance was the only way to escape the overwhelming panic. # Vignette: Hemi

Hemi is a 71-year-old Māori man who has been married to his wife, Aroha, for nearly forty-five years. He works part-time as a cashier at a large supermarket near his home in South Auckland — a job he took on after retiring from construction work, partly to stay busy, partly because he genuinely enjoys talking to people. Or he used to.

About two years ago, Hemi was finishing an evening shift when a young man entered the store and attacked another customer — a woman in her mid-thirties — with a knife, just three registers down from where Hemi was standing. He watched the whole thing unfold in the space of perhaps thirty seconds. He remembers the sound more than anything else: the woman's scream cutting off too quickly, the wet noise he cannot bring himself to describe even now, the way his own voice disappeared when he tried to call out. He was frozen behind his register, hands flat on the counter, unable to move until a colleague pulled him into the back room. The woman survived, but only just.

In the weeks that followed, Hemi told himself he was fine. He is not a man who has ever considered himself fragile. He went back to work after a few days, stood behind his register, and smiled at customers. But something had shifted in a way he could not name at the time. He began scanning every person who walked through the automatic doors — reading their hands, their body language, the shape of their jackets. If someone moved quickly or reached into a bag, his heart would slam against his ribs and he would find himself gripping the counter again, back in that moment, smelling the blood he is certain he could smell even from three registers away.

He stopped sleeping well almost immediately. He lies awake most nights running through what he should have done — shouted a warning, moved toward her, done *something* — even though he knows, on some level, that there was nothing to be done. When he does sleep, he wakes from dreams he cannot fully recall but that leave him drenched and rigid beside Aroha, who has learned not to touch him suddenly in the night.

Hemi has become quieter at home. His grandchildren visit on weekends, and he loves them fiercely, but he finds the noise and chaos of a full house overwhelming in a way it never used to be. He sits apart more often now, watching from the edges. Aroha has noticed. She is a patient woman, but she tells him she misses him — that he is present in the room but somewhere else entirely, and she doesn't know how to reach him.

At work, he has requested a register near the back of the store, away from the entrance. His manager accommodated this without asking questions, and Hemi is grateful for that small mercy. Still, there are days when a particular sound — a shopping basket dropped on the floor, a child shrieking with laughter — will send him somewhere he doesn't want to go, and he has to excuse himself to the stockroom and breathe until the world stops narrowing. He has not told his colleagues why.

He carries a particular kind of shame about all of this. He is a grandfather, a husband, a man who spent decades doing physical labor without complaint. He did not experience the trauma himself — he was not the one who was hurt — and this distinction matters enormously to him, even as it provides no relief. He finds himself thinking about the woman sometimes, wondering whether she still carries it too, whether she knows that a man three registers away has not stopped seeing her fall.

He came to therapy at Aroha's quiet insistence. He sat in the first session with his hands on his knees and said, carefully, that he wasn't sure he deserved to be there.

Malia Somsak is a 57-year-old Thai-American woman who has been married for thirty-one years and operates a small gift and import shop in a mid-sized Pacific Northwest city. She presented for psychological assessment approximately four months after what she describes, haltingly and with long pauses, as the worst period of her life — the sudden, near-fatal illness of her youngest son, then nineteen years old, who was admitted to the intensive care unit following a septic infection that went undetected for several days despite two prior visits to an urgent care clinic.

Malia had brought her son in twice before the hospitalization, each time describing his fever, his confusion, his strange pallor. Each time, she was told he likely had a viral illness and was sent home with instructions to rest and hydrate. On the third visit, he collapsed in the waiting room. What followed were eleven days in which Malia sat beside a hospital bed watching her son receive blood transfusions through IV lines, his arms mapped with bruising from repeated needle insertions, monitors tracking a body that seemed to be failing in real time. She held his hand while nurses adjusted drips and drew blood from his veins. She watched the bags of fluid and the tubing and the needles with the helpless attention of someone trying to understand a language she had never been taught. Her son survived, but the recovery was long, and Malia has not been the same since.

In the months that followed, she found herself unable to describe what had happened in any coherent way. When her husband or close friends asked how she was processing things, she would go quiet, not from reticence but because the words genuinely would not come — she knew what had occurred but could not assemble it into sentences. More disorienting still, she would sometimes be standing behind the counter of her shop, arranging ceramic figurines or counting receipts, and be overtaken by a wave of terror and grief so complete that it left her breathless, with no accompanying image, no clear memory surfacing — just the full weight of those eleven days pressing through her chest without explanation.

She had come to believe, with a certainty that felt immovable, that she had failed her son. The clinic had missed the signs twice, and she had accepted their reassurances and taken him home. She was certain she should have pushed harder, demanded more, refused to leave. Alongside this sat a fury she could not resolve: what happened was deeply unfair, and no one — not the clinic, not any administrator — had acknowledged it or been held accountable. This sense of institutional abandonment had calcified into something she carried daily.

At the shop, where she spends six days a week, the triggers are not abstract. A customer once came in with a bandaged arm and a visible IV port from an outpatient procedure, and Malia had to excuse herself to the back room. She keeps a small first-aid kit behind the counter as she always has, but she can no longer open it — the sight of the sterile packaging and the needle inside is enough to produce a rapid heartbeat and a tightening in her throat. She has rescheduled her own annual physical three times, unable to bring herself to enter a medical building. She asks her husband repeatedly, sometimes several times an evening, whether he thinks she seems healthy, whether he thinks she is okay. She cannot fully explain why his reassurances never quite settle the question for her.

She avoids films, music, and even family gatherings that might stir strong feeling — not just sadness, but anything that moves her, including joy. Her husband has noticed that she seems absent at celebrations, that she leaves the room when their grandchildren become loud with excitement. She has not been able to deliberately revisit the hospitalization in any structured way; when she tries, the memory resists her, remaining formless and inaccessible even as its emotional residue continues to surface unbidden.

What finally brought Malia to seek help was her son's upcoming wedding. She wants to be present for it — truly present — and she is afraid she will not be able to manage the emotions of the day. What she hopes for, she said quietly at the end of the intake, is simply to feel like herself again. What she fears most is that the person she was before those eleven days no longer exists.

Lena, a 57-year-old South Eastern Asian woman who owns a small shop in her neighborhood, has been struggling with the aftermath of an event that left her feeling deeply shaken and vulnerable. The traumatic experience began when her youngest child fell severely ill, nearly losing his life to a rare condition. This period was marked by countless medical procedures, blood tests, and constant vigilance at the hospital. The memory of those dark days still haunts Lena, particularly the sight of needles and medical equipment that now trigger intense anxiety. Every time she sees such items, her body reacts with an immediate surge of adrenaline, her heart racing as if reliving the trauma all over again. The mere thought of undergoing a medical examination or procedure herself is almost unbearable, leading her to avoid any such encounters at all costs. Lena's shop has become both her sanctuary and the stage where these avoidance behaviors play out daily. She often finds herself scanning the shelves and customers for signs that might remind her of the hospital environment she so desperately wants to escape. The sight of a customer with bandages or someone using medical equipment like a blood pressure monitor can trigger her strong physical reactions, leaving her feeling dizzy and disoriented. The memory of what happened is fragmented and difficult to access deliberately. When Lena tries to recall specific moments from that time, she finds it hard to pinpoint the details, yet the emotional intensity remains vivid without clear images. This disconnection between emotion and memory leaves her with a sense of unreality about the events, making it even harder for her to process what occurred. Lena's struggles have taken a toll on both her personal life and her business. She has become increasingly reliant on reassurance from her husband and close friends, constantly seeking validation that she is okay and everything will be fine. This behavior, however, has led to tension in her relationships, as those around her feel burdened by the need for constant support. Avoiding all feelings—both positive and negative—has also become a coping mechanism, which has left Lena feeling emotionally numb. She avoids social gatherings and any activities that might stir up emotions, leading to increased isolation and loneliness. Her business has suffered as well; she often finds herself shutting down during busy periods, unable to engage with customers or manage her daily tasks effectively. Lena's negative appraisals are deeply rooted in a sense of injustice and institutional failure. She feels that the medical system let her family down during their time of need, and this belief has made it even harder for her to trust others or seek help. The weight of feeling that she failed to protect her child adds another layer of guilt and self-blame. The combination of these symptoms has left Lena feeling trapped in a cycle of anxiety and avoidance. She finally decided to seek help when the strain on her relationships and business became too much to bear, realizing that she needed professional guidance to navigate through this turmoil. What frightens her most is the prospect of reliving those traumatic moments again, while what she hopes for most is finding a way to regain control over her life without being constantly haunted by the past.

Marisol García was 47 when she first came to treatment, a married Latin American woman who had spent most of her adult life working in social ministry, moving between parish outreach, food distribution, and home visits with women and families in need. By her own account, she had once been known among friends and co-workers as cheerful and steady, the kind of person who could sit with anyone and make them feel accompanied. That sense of herself changed after she was raped in an encounter she described only in fragments, each fragment arriving in her mind as a separate picture rather than as a continuous story. She could still recall the approach of the evening, the sudden shift in the room, and then brief, frozen moments of what followed, but when she tried to explain it to others she would stop and say she knew what had happened without being able to find the words for it. What returned most vividly was not a narrative but a series of snapshots: a detail of light, the sense of being pinned by fear, the bodily awareness of shame afterward. When she remembered it, she felt overwhelmed by guilt, as if even the fact of remembering carried blame.

In the months after the assault, Marisol noticed that silence had become unbearable. In her apartment, in church corridors after Mass, or in the quiet before starting her ministry visits, an unusual stillness made her chest tighten. She would look up, listening hard, certain that something dangerous was about to happen if the room stayed too quiet. Delays had the same effect. If a person was late to meet her at the parish office, or if a family did not answer the door at the expected time, she immediately assumed that something bad was happening. Even when she knew logically that she was in a safe place, she could not relax her body. She described herself as always braced, unable to let her shoulders drop, as if easing up for even a moment might invite harm. At home, her husband noticed that she kept checking locks and windows and seemed to remain on guard well past the hour when she used to sit down with tea and talk about the day.

Marisol also made changes in the way she handled her body. She began to eat with strict control, choosing very small portions and organizing meals tightly, saying that if she could manage food exactly she could at least feel some measure of control in her life. She became wary of relaxing in the evening, especially after work, and would often stay busy with chores or paperwork rather than sit down. Rest felt risky to her, as if letting herself soften would leave her exposed. Alongside that, she developed a hard inner voice. She told herself she deserved to suffer because of what happened, and she carried that self-punishing belief into ordinary moments, refusing comfort from her husband and feeling she had no right to be soothed. The shame she felt about what had happened to her body was particularly painful; she spoke of it with visible distress, as though the assault had left a mark on her womanhood that she could not bear to name directly.

These changes began to affect her ministry work in concrete ways. Marisol still reported for duty, but she became less present during visits and more preoccupied with the tone of a room, especially whether conversations had gone oddly quiet. In a ministry kitchen, the sudden hush after a burst of activity could pull her attention away from the women she was serving. If a family was running late to a scheduled appointment, she would wait with growing dread, convinced something terrible was unfolding. Over time, she pulled back from moments that used to restore her, avoiding sitting still after long days and filling every gap with errands or service tasks. This left her more exhausted and less connected to the people around her, which distressed her deeply because she had entered social ministry precisely to be close to others.

By the time she sought help, Marisol described feeling that she was no longer the woman she had been. She said, with a quiet finality, that she used to be happy but now was always miserable, and that she had lost faith in people, in life, and in God’s protection. What brought her in was not one single episode but the accumulation of these changes: the constant vigilance in silence, the panic when time passed too slowly, the inability to let herself rest, and the way guilt and shame met her every time the memory surfaced. She said she wanted to stop living as though danger were always about to break in, and she hoped for a way to feel safe in her own body again, though what frightened her most was the possibility that she might never recover the trust and peace she once had.

Kai was seventy-one years old and had worked as a cashier at a grocery store for nearly fifteen years. He was a large, soft-spoken man from Oceania who had built a quiet life in a midwestern American town with his wife of forty years. That life had been stable, predictable, until the afternoon he walked into the bank on his day off. He had only needed to deposit a check. He was standing in line when a man in a hooded jacket walked through the door and pulled a handgun from his waistband. Kai remembered the sound of the door opening—that specific hydraulic hiss and click—and then the shouting. He remembered the way the gun moved, the way people dropped to the floor. He remembered the silence afterward, the way his own hands shook when he finally walked out. But beyond those fragments, the rest was missing. When he tried to tell his wife what happened, he lost the thread halfway through, his sentences collapsing into silence. He could not tell a clear story of what had happened, even to himself. The memory felt like a series of disconnected photographs with no narrative holding them together.

In the weeks that followed, Kai began to notice changes he could not explain. He started flinching at unexpected movement—a customer reaching suddenly for a wallet, a child darting past his register. He found himself watching people closely, scanning their hands, their eyes, their postures, certain that someone in the store might be preparing to harm him. He was always on guard now, his body tight, his gaze moving constantly. The sound of a door opening or slamming became unbearable; each time the automatic doors at the grocery store hissed open, his heart would slam against his ribs, and he would feel a surge of adrenaline that left him dizzy. He had come to believe that the people who should have protected him—the bank security, the police, the system itself—had failed. No one had been held accountable. The man had never been caught. That institutional failure sat inside Kai like a stone, and it made the world feel fundamentally unsafe. The more he believed that no one was looking out for him, the more vigilant he became, and the more the memories of that afternoon intruded, fragmented and incoherent, each fragment reinforcing his sense that something terrible could happen again at any moment.

The triggers and the memories fed each other in a cycle Kai could not escape. A baby crying in the checkout line would send him back to the bank, to the sound of a woman sobbing on the floor, and he would feel that familiar deadness spread through his chest—the emotional numbness that had settled over him like a fog. He had stopped feeling much of anything, and that frightened him more than the hypervigilance did. He was certain that if he let himself feel what had happened, he would fall apart completely. So he stayed numb, and the numbness made the memories even harder to grasp. Without emotional connection, the story of what happened remained disjointed, a collection of shards he could not assemble. And because he could not assemble them, they seemed to multiply, triggered by the smallest sounds and movements, which only made him more watchful, more certain that danger was everywhere.

His wife noticed that he no longer joined her for their evening walks. He made excuses—his knees hurt, he was tired—but the truth was that he could not bear the unpredictability of being outside. A car door slamming, a dog barking, a jogger appearing suddenly around a corner: each sound or movement felt like an ambush. At work, he had started asking for the register farthest from the entrance, the one with a wall at his back. His manager had raised an eyebrow but said nothing. Kai knew he was becoming a different person, but he did not know how to stop it. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at the grocery store when a toddler dropped a sippy cup and the plastic clatter against the floor sent him into a full panic attack. He had to excuse himself to the break room, where he sat shaking for twenty minutes. That night, he told his wife he could not go on like this. What he was most afraid of, he said, was that he would never feel safe again—that the rest of his life would be spent bracing for a disaster that had already happened.

The incident unfolded on a rain-slicked service road behind the veterinary hospital where Samir worked the night shift. A stranger had stepped from the shadows of the ambulance bay, pressing a knife against his ribs while the engine’s diesel fumes and the mugger’s sour breath flooded the alley. When Samir had frozen, he had felt the cold metal and the sudden, violent violation of his personal space. That moment of terror became the anchor for everything that followed. Over the next few weeks, the assault refused to stay contained. The olfactory recall would strike without warning in the exam room when a client’s cheap cologne or the antiseptic cleaner caught the breeze, instantly dragging Samir back to the alley. When trying to explain the breakdown to his partner, Samir would lose the thread entirely, hands trembling as the narrative fractured. This involuntary memory intrusion directly fed his negative appraisals; each unbidden flashback convinced him he had permanently lost his happiness and that he could no longer rely on others to keep him safe. Consequently, his constant vigilance took over. He found himself scanning every crowded street for threatening postures and checking behind him whenever footsteps echoed, even at home where he felt perpetually alert and trapped. His professional environment quickly became a minefield. During a routine surgery, a sudden drop in a medical instrument’s metal tray triggered a full somatic memory of the mugger’s grip. The threat system hijacked his response: instead of calling for help, Samir adopted a fawn response, becoming overly compliant and apologetic to the anesthesiologist until the panic subsided. This maladaptive strategy, combined with his growing belief that the world was fundamentally unpredictable, drove him to avoid going out entirely. He began calling in sick, rationalizing that if he stayed indoors and pretended the event hadn’t been that severe, he might eventually stop feeling terrified. However, this avoidance only intensified his physiological scanning. By refusing to leave his apartment, his nervous system remained stuck in a defensive loop, making every minor noise feel like a precursor to violence. The more he tried to dismiss the trauma, the more his negative appraisals hardened, convincing him that he had to be especially careful because danger was inevitable. These beliefs, in turn, kept his memory systems hypersensitive; his mind braced for threat so constantly that it misfired, turning ordinary stimuli into full traumatic recalls. The isolation strained his relationship, and the weight of his unprocessed symptoms finally forced him into our intake office. He had come to believe that his former optimism was gone, replaced by a relentless need to monitor his surroundings for danger. What frightened him most was that his avoidance had made him a ghost in his own career, leaving him uncertain if he could ever return to treating animals or trusting his own perception of reality. He sat now, hands folded tightly in his lap, hoping for a way to untangle the memories without losing his livelihood, and dreading the thought that his hypervigilance might never quiet down.

Parisa is a 26-year-old non-binary veterinarian of Iranian descent who presented for psychological assessment approximately four months after being mugged at knifepoint outside a convenience store near their apartment. It was a Tuesday evening in late autumn; Parisa had stopped to buy supplies on the way home from a long clinic shift. A man approached from behind, pressed something cold and sharp against their ribs, and demanded their phone and wallet. What Parisa remembers most viscerally is not the knife but the smell — cigarette smoke and something chemical, like cleaning fluid — and the sound of their own voice coming out thin and compliant, saying "okay, okay, take it, please." Within seconds the man was gone. Parisa stood on the pavement for a long moment, then walked home, and told themselves, as they unlocked the door, that it had not really been that serious. Nobody had been hurt. It was over.

That minimisation — the insistence that the event was not that bad — offered brief relief but quietly prevented Parisa from processing what had happened. Over the following weeks, they noticed that any time they tried to explain the mugging to their partner or a colleague, the thread of the account dissolved; they would lose the sequence, trail off, and change the subject. The memory had not been laid down as a coherent narrative but as fragments: the pressure against their ribs, the smell, the sound of their own compliance. Because the memory remained disorganised and unresolved, it was easily ambushed by the environment. At the veterinary clinic where Parisa works, the sharp smell of antiseptic solution — a routine and unavoidable feature of the job — could instantly collapse the distance between then and now, flooding them with the full sensory weight of that evening. In those moments, still in scrubs and mid-procedure, Parisa would feel their heart hammering and their eyes begin to sweep the room.

That reflexive scanning had become near-constant. Parisa now checked behind themselves when walking between the parking lot and the clinic entrance, and remained alert even inside their own home, sitting with their back to the wall and listening to sounds in the hallway. They had come to believe, with quiet but firm conviction, that the world was fundamentally unpredictable and threatening — that you simply could not know what was coming next, and that being caught unguarded once was proof that vigilance was the only rational response. This heightened threat monitoring, however, kept the nervous system in a state of perpetual readiness that made intrusive recall far more likely: a shadow in the peripheral vision, a stranger's footstep behind them on the pavement, and the memory would surge back unbidden, sometimes with the smell arriving before any visual image.

The appraisals that had settled around the event were bleak and generalising. Parisa had come to feel that the person who had once moved through the world with relative ease and warmth was simply gone — that they used to be happy, and now were not, and that this was a permanent condition rather than a symptom. Alongside this was a corrosive sense that other people could not be relied upon: no one had intervened that evening, and their attempts to explain what happened had been met with what felt like inadequate understanding. These beliefs fed directly into Parisa's avoidance of going out, which had narrowed their life considerably. They drove to work and drove home; they no longer walked anywhere after dark. Their partner had begun to notice, and the resulting conversations — gentle but persistent — had started to feel like another demand for compliance, another situation in which Parisa found themselves agreeing and accommodating in order to reduce tension rather than from genuine desire.

The magical thinking that the event had not really been serious remained a recurring retreat, but it carried a cost: each time Parisa minimised what had happened, the memory stayed unintegrated and the threat appraisals went unchallenged, leaving the whole system intact and tightening. The belief that the world was dangerous kept Parisa scanning; the scanning kept triggering memory fragments; the memory fragments reinforced the belief that danger was everywhere and that they were permanently changed by it.

What finally brought Parisa to seek help was a moment at the clinic when, smelling the antiseptic as a colleague cleaned an instrument tray, they froze completely in front of a client and could not speak for nearly a minute. They were afraid, they said quietly at intake, that they were losing their ability to do the one thing that had always felt like solid ground. What they most hoped for was to stop feeling like a stranger in their own life.

She is 45, a Middle Eastern woman who now lives alone in a quiet apartment and works as an auditor, a job she chose partly because numbers stay where they are put. In her work, columns reconcile or they do not. There is comfort in that. People at the office know her as exacting, reserved, and reliable, someone who catches small discrepancies others miss. They do not see how much effort it takes for her to sit with her back to a glass conference room wall, or how often she scans for exits before taking her seat.

When she speaks about the war, she does not begin with politics or ideology. She begins with sound. She remembers the whistle before impact, the way everyone around her would go silent for half a second as if the body understood danger before the mind could name it. In her late twenties, she is attached to a military logistics unit in a combat zone, helping track supplies, fuel, and personnel movements. Even then, she works with lists, inventories, and shortages. Her role is not on the front line, but no one where she is feels far from it. Roads are mined. Convoys do not always return complete. Buildings that seem ordinary in the morning become piles of concrete by noon.

One afternoon, she is in a crowded operations building checking manifests when an explosion hits nearby with enough force to throw her against a wall. The room fills with dust so thick she cannot see her own hands. She hears screaming, then a strange ringing, then another blast farther off. For a few moments she believes the ceiling is coming down. She tastes blood where she has bitten her tongue. Someone is calling for help. Someone else is shouting names. She crawls because standing feels impossible, and when the dust clears enough, she sees a young man she knows from transport lying twisted under part of a collapsed partition. She remembers his boot first, then his face. For years afterward, that sequence returns to her against her will.

After that day, she keeps functioning because everyone around her keeps functioning. She works longer, sleeps in fragments, startles at every metallic bang. She tells herself this is normal in war. The more frightened she feels, the more tightly she controls the details she can control. She checks supply counts repeatedly. She rewrites logs to make them neat. She stops laughing with others over tea because laughter now feels reckless, almost disrespectful. At night she lies awake in uniform, too tense to undress fully, listening for engines and shelling. If she dozes, she wakes with her heart racing, disoriented, already bracing.

When she eventually leaves the combat setting, she expects relief to arrive with distance. Instead, ordinary civilian life feels unreal and unsafe in a different way. In markets, crowded aisles make her sweat. Fireworks send her to the floor before she knows what she is doing. The smell of diesel exhaust can transport her so quickly that she is no longer in the present but back in that building, breathing dust, searching through debris. She avoids news footage, avoids talking about the war, avoids former colleagues who might ask what she remembers. Her family interprets her silence as strength at first, then as coldness. She marries, hoping routine will settle her, but her husband grows weary of her vigilance. She checks locks repeatedly, wakes him by shaking him after nightmares, insists on knowing exactly when he will return if he goes out. When he approaches her unexpectedly from behind, she flinches hard enough to knock over a glass or shove him away. She feels ashamed immediately, then angry at herself for seeming fragile. Over time, the marriage narrows around what cannot be said, and eventually it ends.

In her current job, she is respected, but her competence is built around constant strain. She arrives early so she can choose the seat that gives her the clearest view of the room. She keeps spreadsheets immaculate and feels a surge of panic when there is an unexplained discrepancy, as if one missing receipt could open into catastrophe. During site visits, if she hears construction noise or a truck backfire, her body jolts before her mind catches up. She will excuse herself to the restroom, grip the sink, and wait for the pounding in her chest to slow. Sometimes she splashes water on her face and studies herself in the mirror with irritation, as though fear is a personal failure she should have audited out of her system by now.

Her nights remain the hardest. Sleep comes late and breaks easily. In dreams, she is back in the operations building, or on a road waiting for an explosion she knows is coming. She wakes drenched, her jaw aching from clenching. In the morning she is exhausted but unwilling to rest, because being tired feels safer than lying still with her thoughts. She keeps her apartment orderly, almost spare. Sudden visitors unsettle her. She rarely socializes unless necessary, and even with relatives she loves, she sits near the door and listens past the conversation for sounds outside.

What troubles her most is not only fear but the way the war has rearranged her inner life. She used to think of herself as warm, sociable, capable of pleasure. Now she feels cut off from other people, as if some essential part of her remains standing in dust and noise, unable to move forward. She tells her story carefully, in pieces, then apologizes for becoming emotional. But even in the apology there is something revealing: she has spent years trying to contain an experience that does not stay contained.

Patient Vignette: Dr. Miguel Torres

Dr. Miguel Torres, a 70-year-old widowed dentist of Latin American descent, sits carefully on the edge of the chair in my office, his posture rigid and his hands resting motionless on his knees. He arrives precisely on time for each session, dressed in a pressed button-down shirt, and he apologizes twice before sitting down. He is here at the urging of his daughter, who noticed he has not been the same since the anniversary last month of the bombing.

The event that changed everything happened five years ago, on a Tuesday morning that began like any other. Miguel had just finished a root canal on a young mother and was walking to the front desk of his dental practice to review the afternoon schedule. The building shook with a sound he describes not as a noise, but as a physical blow—a pressure that slammed into his chest and threw him against the wall. A car bomb had detonated two blocks away, targeting a government building. For the next several hours, Miguel was trapped in his office with three patients and his hygienist. The windows blew inward. The ceiling tiles fell. Dust filled the air so thickly that he could not see his own hands. He remembers the screaming, the smell of ozone and plaster, and the terrible, silent pause when he thought the second bomb was coming.

In the weeks that followed, Miguel returned to work. He told himself he was fine. He told his wife, Elena, that he was lucky. But he began to notice small changes. He stopped driving past the intersection where the bomb had occurred, even if it meant adding twenty minutes to his commute. He began checking the exits in every room he entered—the grocery store, the pharmacy, his own living room. When a patient would flinch unexpectedly in the chair, his heart would pound so hard he could hear it in his ears.

Elena died two years ago from cancer. In the months after her death, Miguel’s vigilance became a full-time occupation. He now lives alone in the house they shared for forty years. He has retired from dentistry, though he keeps his license active. The retirement was not entirely voluntary. During his last year of practice, he found himself unable to tolerate the sound of the high-speed drill. It reminded him too much of the ringing in his ears after the blast. He would freeze mid-procedure, his hand shaking, the drill whining in his patient’s mouth. He referred his remaining patients to a younger colleague and locked the door to his office.

Now, he spends most of his days in a careful routine. He wakes at 6:00 a.m., checks the locks on all the doors twice, and then sits in his recliner with a cup of coffee. He watches the news but cannot tolerate certain images—smoke, crowds, men in uniforms running. He avoids the anniversary of the bombing and the date of Elena’s death. He no longer attends his weekly domino game with friends from the neighborhood, because the noise of the tiles being slapped on the table makes him jump. He has not been to the local market in over a year; his daughter does his shopping.

He tells me he feels like a ghost in his own life. He is irritable with his grandchildren, snapping at them for no reason. He has nightmares where he is back in the dark office, feeling for the door, and he wakes up in a sweat, convinced he hears footsteps. He is tired all the time, but he cannot sleep. He is ashamed of his fear. He was a man who fixed broken teeth, who calmed anxious children, who served his community. Now, he is a man who cannot walk into a crowded room without checking the exits. He does not use the word trauma. He says, “I just haven’t been the same since that day.”

# Anh's Reckoning

Anh Tran was twenty-two when the earthquake hit Manila in the early morning of April 15th, 2022. He had been there for a three-week internship at a tech startup, staying in a corporate housing unit on the twenty-third floor of a mixed-use building in Makati. He had been asleep when the first tremor woke him—a deep, rolling sensation that made the windows rattle and his laptop slide off the desk. For the first few seconds, he thought it would pass. Then the building began to sway in earnest, and the sound came: a groaning, twisting noise from the structure itself, like the building was breathing in pain. The floor tilted. His bed slid across the room. He scrambled to the doorframe, gripping it as the tremors intensified, and in those endless seconds he became certain the building would collapse. The taste of his own blood filled his mouth—he had bitten his cheek hard enough to draw it, though he had no memory of doing so. When the shaking finally stopped, after what felt like an eternity but was only ninety seconds, Anh sat on the floor of his apartment with that metallic taste still coating his tongue, his neck screaming with tension from bracing himself against the doorframe, his hands shaking so violently he could not hold them still.

He made it out of the building. The stairwells were chaos—people pushing, crying, the smell of dust and fear. His neck felt wrenched, but he descended all twenty-three flights and walked out onto a street transformed. The city was fractured: buildings with their facades peeled away, cars crushed, people wandering in shock. He spent that day in a makeshift shelter, and the next day he was on a flight home to San Diego.

The memories did not feel real. In the weeks after, Anh would lie awake at night trying to convince himself it had actually happened. The scale of it—the building swaying, the real possibility of death—seemed too extreme to be true. His mind kept rejecting it, turning it over like something counterfeit. Yet his body remembered with absolute clarity. Whenever his neck stiffened—from sitting at his desk, from sleeping wrong, from tension—a specific sensation would flood back: the taste of blood, the feeling of the floor moving beneath him, the terror of weightlessness. Sometimes the emotion came without any image at all, just a wave of dread and certainty that something catastrophic was about to happen, and he would not even know what had triggered it until minutes later, when he realized his neck had tightened slightly or he had felt a small vibration from a truck passing outside.

Anh returned to his job as a UX designer at a mid-sized software firm in San Diego, but something had fractured in him that could not be simply reset. He found himself unable to trust the reassurances people offered him. A colleague told him the building was probably fine, that he was lucky, that he should be grateful. Anh heard the words but could not accept them. People were not what they seemed; they did not understand, they could not understand, and their attempts to comfort him felt hollow and false. He began to isolate himself, eating lunch alone, declining after-work drinks, working from home more often than the office allowed. His manager asked if he was all right. Anh said yes, but the truth was darker: he felt set apart from everyone around him, as if he had crossed into a world they could not see and could never fully return from. He no longer belonged in the ordinary rhythms of his team's life. When his coworkers joked about the office building's structural integrity, he said nothing, but inside he was certain they had no idea how fragile everything was, how quickly the ground could betray you.

By month four, he was working from home almost exclusively. He had not been back to the office in three weeks. His manager had begun asking pointed questions about his commitment. Anh knew he was failing, but the thought of being in that building—any tall building—made his chest tight and his neck tense. The taste would come. The unreality would settle over him. He would spend the afternoon convinced that something terrible was about to happen, waiting for the next tremor, certain it was coming.

Last week, after a particularly severe episode where he could not work for an entire day, Anh finally reached out to a therapist. He told his parents, who had been worried but unsure how to help. He said he needed to understand why the memory would not feel real, why his body kept insisting something catastrophic was imminent, and why he could not seem to connect with anyone anymore. What frightened him most was not the memory itself, but the possibility that he would spend the rest of his life feeling this way—untethered from reality, separated from everyone he knew, waiting for the next disaster that his body was certain was coming.

Two years ago, Lian’s youngest child collapsed at school and was rushed to the county hospital. She remembered the sterile corridor, the rhythmic hiss of monitoring equipment, and the way multiple IV lines were threaded into his thin arms. Doctors drew blood repeatedly, the needles glinting under fluorescent lights as nurses adjusted the dripping fluids. When his condition worsened, he required another procedure to clear his airway. She stood watching the medical equipment roll past, feeling utterly powerless. The care had been fragmented; specialists changed shifts without thorough handoffs, and when the family raised concerns about the delay in his stabilization, they were met with clipped responses and closed doors. She had come to believe that what happened to her was deeply unfair and nothing had been done about it. She also believed that the people or institutions that should have protected her let them down. She kept replaying the hours he lay unresponsive, certain that she should have protected others and that she had failed. In the months that followed, these appraisals settled alongside a constellation of experiences that occupied her days. She was unable to relax even when she knew she was in a safe place, her shoulders perpetually drawn tight. Her eyes constantly scanned the surroundings for signs of danger, tracking every passing car or distant siren. When a loud truck backfired outside her home, her chest tightened and her hands trembled, a strong physical reaction when something reminded her of the stressful experience. She tried to erase the memory of the event, changing her daily routes, discarding old hospital paperwork, and refusing to look at photographs from that period. She avoided anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, staying meticulously occupied at her grocery shop to prevent any emotional surge. When she tried to deliberately recall what happened, she found it difficult to access the memory; the facts remained known, but she was unable to find words to describe it. Instead, she would be caught off guard by a full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, leaving her breathless and disoriented. She kept asking others to reassure her that she was okay, asking her husband repeatedly to confirm that she was alright, that she was not broken, that they were safe. Each reassurance helped only until the next morning, when the tension returned. Now, at her dry goods shop in a quiet commercial strip, these habits had become her daily reality. When a regular customer sliced his palm on a cardboard box, the sight of the blood made her stomach lurch and her shoulders lock. She stepped back behind the counter, her pulse hammering, and forced herself to call a first-aid kit without looking directly at the wound. The last time she tried to schedule her annual physical, the thought of undergoing a medical examination or procedure unraveled her completely; she cancelled the appointment and has not booked another since. Her husband noticed how she flinches at his bandages, how they avoid discussing the hospital visit altogether, and how their conversations have narrowed to logistics to keep any feeling at bay. The shop’s steady rhythm has become her anchor, yet she watches the front door every time the bell chimes, certain that another crisis could arrive at any moment. She finally came to therapy because the silence inside her shop had grown louder than the fear, and because she could no longer carry the weight of a system she believed had failed them alone. What she hopes for is simply to stop bracing for a blow that has already fallen, and what frightened her most was that the dread might never let go.

# Maria's Story

Maria sits in the worn leather chair, her hands folded carefully in her lap. At forty-seven, she carries herself with the composed dignity of someone accustomed to holding others' pain. For nearly twenty years, she has worked as a social ministry worker in her community, counseling families in crisis, advocating for domestic violence survivors, connecting vulnerable people with resources. Her colleagues describe her as tireless, compassionate, unshakeable. What they don't see is the price she pays for that steadiness.

Three years ago, Maria was assaulted in the parking lot behind the community center where she worked late one evening. A man she had never seen before forced her into her car. The attack lasted perhaps fifteen minutes, though Maria says time felt distorted—sometimes it felt like seconds, sometimes like hours. She remembers the smell of his cologne mixed with sweat, the coldness of the metal door handle against her back, the way her voice wouldn't work when she tried to scream. When he left, she sat frozen in the driver's seat for what might have been minutes or an hour. Eventually, she drove home without reporting it.

She didn't tell anyone for six months. Not her husband, not her supervisor, not the police. She continued going to work, continued listening to other women's stories of violation and survival, all while feeling like an imposter. How could she counsel others when she couldn't even speak about what happened to her? The silence felt safer than the alternative—the questions, the investigation, the exposure.

But the trauma didn't stay contained in that silence. About eight months after the assault, Maria began having trouble sleeping. She would lie awake next to her husband, her body rigid, jumping at every sound. When she did sleep, she had nightmares so vivid she would wake gasping, sometimes striking out at her husband in the darkness. He held her through these episodes with confusion and concern, still not understanding what had happened.

The hypervigilance crept into her days. Parking lots became unbearable. She started parking directly under lights, as close to building entrances as possible, scanning the area before getting out of her car. At the community center, she found herself unable to stay late, making excuses to leave by five o'clock. Her colleagues noticed her withdrawal but attributed it to burnout. The irony wasn't lost on Maria—she recognized the signs of trauma in herself that she saw in her clients every day, yet she remained unable to name it.

Certain sounds trigger her—car doors slamming, unexpected voices, the particular timbre of male laughter. When these sounds occur, her body responds before her mind can catch up. Her heart races, her breathing becomes shallow, and she feels the phantom pressure of hands on her body. She has learned to excuse herself to bathrooms, to take walks, to create distance between herself and whoever is near.

Her marriage has suffered under the weight of unspoken trauma. Her husband senses her distance but doesn't know how to reach across it. Maria finds it difficult to be touched, even affectionately. Sex has become something she endures rather than experiences. She hasn't told him the full truth yet, though she knows she must. The secret has become its own kind of violence, corroding the intimacy they once shared.

What keeps Maria functioning is her work—the very thing that also torments her. She continues to show up for her clients, to listen to their stories, to believe in their capacity to heal. But lately, she wonders if she is simply performing recovery while fracturing privately. She tells herself that other survivors have endured worse, that she should be stronger, that coming forward would only complicate things. Yet the nightmares persist, the hypervigilance deepens, and the isolation grows.

Amina is a 42-year-old divorced African American woman who works long shifts on a factory floor, and she came to treatment after months of feeling as though her life had narrowed to getting through work, getting home, and staying on guard. Years earlier, she was detained and tortured. She describes being held in a small room where other bodies were forced close to hers, where names were shouted back and forth by the men who controlled the space, and where the air carried a distinct odor she can still summon against her will. The weather that day had been heavy and close, the kind of humid pressure before a storm that now turns her stomach. What stays with her is not a coherent story but fragments: the smell, the sense of bodies pressing near, the sound of names, and the certainty that she had no control over what happened to her own body.

In the aftermath, Amina began to notice that certain moments in ordinary life were not ordinary to her. On crowded bus rides or when a coworker at the factory leaned too near to speak over the machinery, her whole body stiffened before she had time to think. If she heard a name that resembled one she associates with the men who hurt her, or if the day turned hot and storm-heavy, she would feel pulled sharply backward into the event. She says that when those things happen, she can sometimes smell again what she smelled then, and the memory arrives with such force and strangeness that it feels unreal, almost as if it happened to somebody else. Because those cues seem to appear anywhere, she has come to see the world as dangerous in a constant, ambient way, not just in obviously unsafe places.

That sense of danger has spread into her view of herself. Amina had once thought of herself as strong, capable, and able to endure hard work without losing her footing. Now she is shaken by how little warning she seems to have before her body reacts. She has come to believe she can no longer trust her own body, and that she is no longer capable in the way she once was. When she startles violently at ordinary noises in the plant or finds herself listening at night for any sound that might mean someone is entering her apartment, it confirms for her that the danger is real and that she has been permanently changed by it. The more she scans, the more she notices sounds, footsteps, weather shifts, and people standing too close; those same things now register immediately as signs of threat.

Over time she has built her days around trying not to be overtaken. She wears heavy makeup every day, describing it less as vanity than as a way to feel hidden and armoured. She avoids clothes that resemble what she wore during the torture, even when that makes getting dressed for work more difficult. She keeps her mind occupied constantly—television on in the background, music in her headphones after work, repetitive mental lists on the assembly line—because any quiet moment risks bringing back the smell, the unreal quality of the memory, and the sickening sense that the past is not fully past. These habits make sense to her because she is convinced that if she lets down her guard or allows herself to think directly about what happened, she will lose control altogether.

At the factory, the cycle is especially tight. The closeness of other workers, shouted names over machinery, and the metallic smells in the heat of the building can all act as triggers. She becomes intensely alert, jumping at routine noises and monitoring every movement around her. In that state, the memory intrudes in sensory flashes rather than narrative form, and because it feels alien and unbelievable even while it is vividly present, she tries harder to push it away by overfocusing on tasks, avoiding certain uniforms and fabrics, and checking how she looks behind a mask of makeup before her shift. Yet the effort to keep the memory at bay seems only to leave it more fragmented and more startling when it returns.

At home, nights are the worst. Amina listens for entry sounds with an intensity that leaves her exhausted. A settling radiator, footsteps in the hallway, rain building in humid weather—each can make her body jerk before she has formed a thought. The startle itself frightens her; it seems proof that her body is unreliable and that she is living in a world where danger can come through any door. That fear makes the triggers feel even more potent and broadens the range of what she avoids. By the time she sought help, she was missing social invitations, feeling increasingly cut off, and struggling to keep steady at work because so much energy went into staying occupied and braced.

She came in after realizing that she was no longer simply remembering what had been done to her; she was organizing her whole life around not feeling it and still being ambushed by it. What frightens her most is the belief that the torture has broken something permanent in her—that her body will always react first, that ordinary closeness and ordinary weather will always carry the past inside them. What she hopes, cautiously, is that she might find a way to live without having to hide from names, from crowds, from heat in the air, and from her own memory.

Leila, a 26-year-old non-binary veterinarian in a long-term relationship, had been working a late shift at a small animal clinic in a busy strip mall when the mugging happened. It was just after closing, and they were carrying the day’s deposits to their car in the rear parking lot when two men came up fast from the shadowed side of the building. One had a hand in his jacket and barked for Leila’s bag; the other stayed close enough that Leila could smell cigarette smoke and cheap cologne, a smell that still comes back with painful clarity when they think about it. Leila remembered the sound of their own voice turning thin and polite, offering the bag immediately, apologizing, trying not to anger anyone. They had gone rigidly compliant, fawning through the fear, because in that moment being agreeable felt safer than resisting. Even now, when they try to explain what happened, they lose the thread partway through and cannot finish the story cleanly; the memory seems to splinter as soon as they begin, and sometimes all they can get out is that it was “bad” before going silent. At other times the whole scene arrives without warning from something ordinary—a man’s shoes in a parking lot, the scrape of tires, a whiff of smoke near a clinic entrance—and in an instant the full memory is back, vivid and body-tight, as if the mugging is happening again.

Since then, Leila has come to believe that life has changed in a permanent and uglier way. They say they used to be a happy person, but now they feel miserable much of the time, and that misery has hardened into the conviction that they have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. They no longer trust other people in the way they used to; strangers feel unpredictable, and even familiar settings feel dangerous in a way they did not before. That belief has reshaped their days. Leila scans their surroundings constantly for signs of danger, checks behind them when walking from the clinic to the parking lot, and keeps one eye on reflections in shop windows or car mirrors. They are still on guard inside their own home, listening for footsteps in the hall and tense at every unexpected sound, as if danger could be waiting just beyond the door. The same fear has made going out increasingly difficult, and they have started turning down evening plans with friends and avoiding unnecessary trips after dark. At work, they now choose routes that let them see who is behind them, and they make a point of arriving and leaving at times when the lot is less empty.

The more Leila tries to stay safe, the more their world seems to shrink around the mugging. When they notice themselves scanning and checking, the memory can rush back with surprising force, bringing with it the smell, the parking lot, and the helplessness of that night. Once the memory appears, they quickly slip into old habits of trying to smooth everything over—being extra compliant with anyone who seems irritated, overexplaining themselves, apologizing too much, and avoiding any confrontation that might feel risky. Afterward, they judge themselves for these habits and feel even less like the person they used to be, as if the event has made them smaller and weaker than they can bear to admit. In those moments, the old thought returns that they cannot rely on other people anyway, and that only constant vigilance keeps them intact. That belief, in turn, keeps them scanning harder, checking more often, and withdrawing further from going out, which leaves more room for the memory to intrude and the sense of danger to deepen. By the time Leila sought help, their relationship had begun to feel the strain of how rarely they wanted to leave home in the evenings, and they were exhausted by the effort of seeming calm while remaining braced for the next threat. What brought them in now was the fear that this way of living would become permanent, and what they most hope for is some way to feel safe again without having to keep watch every second.

Ethan was thirty-four, a firefighter in a mid-sized Midwestern city, married for seven years to a schoolteacher named Laura. Four years ago, he had volunteered for a two-month deployment as a civilian relief worker in a conflict zone—a decision he had made believing his emergency training would be useful. The specifics he still avoided revisiting: a convoy ambush near a checkpoint, then the chaotic aftermath of an explosion in a crowded market where he had helped pull bodies from debris. What stayed with him most was the moment when a local woman grabbed his arm, begging for help, and he had felt a surge of protective warmth—only to see her collapse seconds later from shrapnel wounds. That surge of positive emotion, he had since concluded, had made him less alert, more vulnerable. He had learned to push those feelings away immediately.

Back home, the routines of firefighting helped at first. But soon he noticed that even inside his own house, he was on guard. In the living room, he positioned his chair so that he could see both doorways. He would tense whenever a stranger approached him at the grocery store—a neighbor asking for directions felt like a potential threat. In every building, his eyes automatically scanned for exits; he had become so practiced that he noted the fire escape routes within seconds of entering a restaurant or a hardware store. His colleagues at the firehouse began to comment on his rigid posture during downtime.

The maladaptive strategies he adopted only made things worse. He stopped running—his longtime stress release—because the open streets felt exposed, full of unpredictable people. Without that outlet, his vigilance sharpened rather than softened. He developed a habit of sitting near any exit when he was out, and that very habit kept his focus locked on escape routes, which in turn kept his threat-detection system humming. At home, when Laura tried to hold his hand or laugh at a sitcom, he would deliberately flatten his mood. He would remind himself that feeling good was dangerous—it had been the moment he let his guard down in the war zone that had cost that woman her life. Pushing away positive emotions made him feel safer momentarily, but the emotional numbing left him more alone, more on edge, more convinced that the world was hostile. He began to monitor Laura’s movements too, feeling a spike of alarm if she walked up behind him unexpectedly.

These routines solidified over months. He stopped going to the gym altogether, which meant his physical tension had nowhere to go except to fuel his hypervigilance. At work, during a routine call to a house fire, he caught himself scanning the burning building’s exits rather than focusing on the hose line—a dangerous shift that his captain noticed and pulled him aside for. Ethan could not explain why the memory of a market half a world away felt more immediate than the flames in front of him.

What finally drove him to seek help was a sequence of small failures: he snapped at a stranger in a parking lot who merely walked too close; he missed a family dinner because he could not bring himself to sit in a booth that did not offer a clear escape path; he woke Laura at three in the morning because he had been lying still, eyes wide, checking every shadow. His marriage was beginning to strain, and he was terrified that his own hypervigilance was making him a hazard on the job. The sheer brutality of what transpired sometimes makes the story feel unreal, too extreme to have possibly happened within her own lived experience. The world Nia inhabits now is fundamentally different. She has come to believe the world is a profoundly dangerous place, a conviction that colors every interaction and decision. Her body, once a dependable tool for her physically demanding factory work, now feels utterly unreliable, prone to sudden, overwhelming surges of fear that bypass conscious thought. This pervasive sense of threat manifests in her daily life. At home, every creak of the old house or distant siren sends her heart racing. Her body often reacts to perceived danger before her mind has even had time to register what is happening; a sudden jolt, a rapid intake of breath, a pounding pulse, all occur before she consciously identifies a potential threat. Ordinary sounds, like a dropped tool on the factory floor or a car backfiring outside her apartment, make her jump violently, leaving her shaken and hyper-alert for minutes afterward.

Nia has developed several strategies to manage her internal turmoil. She applies heavy makeup each morning, a thick, protective mask she feels can hide the fear in her eyes and the exhaustion etched on her face, making her feel less vulnerable to the scrutiny of others. Her factory job, with its constant noise and repetitive tasks, provides a double-edged sword. The steady hum of machinery can be a form of mental distraction, helping her to focus away from intrusive thoughts. However, the close proximity of co-workers, especially when they brush past her in the narrow aisles, can trigger an intense surge of panic, bringing back the suffocating feeling of confinement and unwanted physical closeness. She finds herself meticulously planning her movements to avoid accidental bumps or touches from colleagues, often taking longer routes around the factory floor.

Over weeks and months, these coping mechanisms have taken a toll. Her hypervigilance and jumpiness have impacted her efficiency at the factory, leading to a recent warning from her supervisor about her declining focus and increased errors. The cumulative exhaustion and the fear of losing her job—her last bastion of independence, even if she feels increasingly incapable—finally pushed her to seek help. Nia is tired of living in a state of constant alert, haunted by a memory that feels both intimately hers and utterly alien, desperate to find a way to trust her own body and the world again.

Javier’s fears were palpable. He was terrified that the memories would never fade, that he would remain trapped in this cycle of anxiety and despair. He doesn’t remember her name. She told it to him twice that evening, first at the parish soup kitchen where she was serving, then again when he followed her out to the parking lot. He called her *mamacita* and *güerita* and she corrected him both times. *Marina*, she said. *My name is Marina.*

That night, after the shift ended, he was waiting by her car. She thought he wanted to thank her for the meal. Instead, he pushed her into the back seat and held a knife against her rib cage. She kept her eyes open the whole time—on the cracked vinyl ceiling, on the streetlight through the fogged glass, on the crucifix dangling from the rearview mirror that swung and swung and never stopped moving.

That was seven years ago last November.

Marina still closes her eyes when she sees a crucifix. It’s not a conscious thing. Her husband, Tomás, notices when they sit in the third pew at Sunday Mass—she shifts her gaze, drops her chin, fumbles with the hem of her sleeve. He thinks she’s praying. She lets him think that.

She works at the diocese now, coordinating emergency aid for migrant families. It’s the same building where the soup kitchen used to run, though they moved the pantry to a different wing after the incident. Marina requested the transfer herself. She told the director it was for efficiency, but really it was because she couldn’t walk past that stretch of parking lot without her palms sweating and her heart slamming against her sternum like a trapped bird. She still can’t. She enters through the side door now, always during daylight, always with a colleague. If she has to leave after dark, she asks someone to walk her. She says it’s because of the neighborhood.

She doesn’t tell them why she really can’t stand the dark anymore, or why she flinches when a car door slams two blocks away, or why she stopped driving a sedan and bought a truck with an automatic lock that beeps three times. The beep is loud, and she presses the button three or four times before she’s sure.

Tomás knows something happened. She told him it was a mugging. That was easier—a faceless stranger, a stolen purse, a quick shove. No mention of the knife. No mention of the weight of his chest against her back. No mention of how she kept whispering *Hail Marys* into the upholstery, but God didn’t answer, and she hasn’t finished a full rosary since.

In their bedroom, she sleeps on the far edge of the mattress, turned away from the door. She used to love his arm draped over her waist; now she tenses at any touch from behind. He thinks she’s just getting older, getting colder. She lets him think that.

At work, she is efficient. She organizes food boxes, fills out forms, listens to mothers tell stories of crossing the border. Their stories are full of violence, but she listens without flinching. She is good at that. It’s the only place she feels anything close to control. But when a young man with dark eyes and a heavy accent thanks her with a hand on her forearm, she pulls away so fast the coffee sloshes onto her sleeve. She apologizes. She says she’s clumsy.

She dreams about the rearview mirror. She dreams about the crucifix. In the dreams, she is still in the back seat, but now she is older, and the man is younger, and the knife is gone, but she cannot open the door. She wakes with her teeth clenched and her hands balled into fists under the pillow.

Last week, she found herself standing in the parking lot at dusk, staring at the exact spot. She didn’t remember walking there. She stood for maybe a minute, then turned around and went back inside. She told the secretary she forgot her keys. The secretary said, *You’re shaking, Marina.* Marina said she was just cold.

She doesn’t cry about it. She hasn’t cried about it since the first month, when she sat in the shower with her clothes on and let the water run cold. Now she just feels tired. Heavy. Like someone filled her bones with lead.

She goes to Mass on Sundays. She crosses herself at the holy water. She kneels. She stares at the altar, but she does not look at the crucifix.

She does not know how to tell Tomás that God didn’t hear her that night, and that maybe that’s the part she can’t forgive.

He is a 70-year-old Latin American man who has spent most of his life in close contact with other people’s pain, first learning to steady his hands as a young dentist and later becoming known in his community as someone calm, precise, and hard to rattle. That self-understanding changed the day of the bombing.

He remembers the morning with unusual clarity: the ordinary sounds of the office, the low hum of the drill, the smell of antiseptic, the familiar rhythm of patients coming and going. Terrorism had always seemed like something that happened elsewhere, in newspapers or on television, until it arrived in the form of a blast that shattered the building and the sense that the world obeys any rules at all. In the moment before impact, he is focused on a simple task at the chairside. In the moment after, he is on the floor, ears ringing, mouth full of dust, unable to make sense of the cries around him. Glass is everywhere. The room that had been carefully ordered minutes before is broken into fragments. He searches for colleagues and patients with a kind of stunned professionalism, as if his training might still matter in a place that has become unrecognizable.

In the days that follow, he functions because there is no other choice. He helps identify the injured, answers questions, fills out forms, calls family members, and returns to work as soon as he can tolerate being inside the building. Yet even then, he begins to notice that something in him remains at the site of the explosion. He startles at sudden noises, especially the sharp pop of balloons, construction bangs, or any unexpected metal sound. His body responds before his mind can catch up: his shoulders rise, his chest tightens, and for a moment he is back in the chaos of that day. He avoids the damaged side of town whenever possible and begins taking longer routes home. He no longer likes sitting with his back to a room, something he never used to think about.

As a dentist, he has always relied on fine motor control and concentration, but after the bombing he finds himself checking and rechecking simple steps. He worries about leaving instruments out, about locked doors, about whether he has heard the office alarm. He becomes more cautious with patients who come in agitated or loud, and he notices that he is less patient than he once was. At times, when he leans over a patient and the suction sounds too loud or the mask feels too tight, he has a brief sensation that he cannot breathe. He blinks, steadies himself, and carries on, though afterward he feels embarrassed by how much effort it takes to remain composed.

Night is harder than day. He falls asleep exhausted, then wakes suddenly from dreams he cannot always remember in detail but that leave him drenched in sweat and disoriented, with the feeling that the bombing is happening again. He lies awake listening to the house settle, scanning the dark for danger. Since the death of his wife several years earlier, the silence at home has been difficult in a different way; after the attack, it becomes almost unbearable. She had been his main witness and source of comfort, the person who would have understood his need to talk through every detail. Without her, he keeps much of it inside. He speaks politely to his adult children and says he is “fine,” though they notice he is more withdrawn and less willing to join family gatherings, especially if they are held in crowded places.

He continues working because retirement feels too empty, and because the office gives him structure. Still, he senses that the event has narrowed his world. He is less likely to accept invitations, less likely to travel, and more likely to sit with old news in the background just for company, even if reports of attacks or violence make him tense. He remains proud of his competence, but he also knows that his confidence is no longer effortless. The bombing has made him alert in ways that never fully turn off, as if some part of him is always listening for the next explosion.
