Amir was twenty-three when it happened, three years ago now, walking home from the veterinary clinic where they worked as an associate. It was early evening in late September, that particular quality of dusk where the light drains fast and the streets empty quickly. They had been turning onto their street in a neighbourhood they had lived in for two years, a place that felt safe enough, when two figures emerged from behind a parked car. One grabbed Amir from behind—an arm around the neck, sudden and absolute—while the other demanded the phone, the wallet, anything of value. The smell hit first: stale cigarette smoke mixed with something chemical and sour, a scent Amir would later struggle to name but could never forget. There was no resistance possible; Amir's body went rigid, compliant, offering up everything without a word. The whole thing lasted perhaps ninety seconds. No weapon was shown. No one was hurt. But something essential shifted in those ninety seconds, something that Amir has spent three years trying to convince themselves did not really happen, or was not that bad—a story they still half-believe on the good days.

Now twenty-six, Amir returned to work in the weeks after because staying home felt worse. But the clinic, which had always been a refuge, became a minefield of invisible triggers. A client's cologne—sharp, chemical—would arrive before the person did, and suddenly Amir was back on that street, the smell crowding out everything else. A dog's sudden lunge during an examination would send Amir's heart into a panic that took hours to settle. The sound of a car door slamming in the parking lot would make Amir flinch, their body tensing as though the threat were immediate and present. Most difficult were the moments between patients, when Amir would find themselves staring out the clinic window at the parking lot, scanning the figures moving past, watching for the particular posture or gait of someone who meant harm. Dr. Patel, the senior veterinarian, noticed the change. Amir had always been confident with animals, quick to make decisions, willing to speak up in team meetings. Now Amir moved through the clinic like a ghost, apologizing for minor mistakes, deferring to every suggestion, becoming almost invisible. When Dr. Patel asked if everything was okay, Amir's throat closed. The words would not come—there was too much, too tangled, and by the time they tried to explain, the thread had vanished and they were standing there mute and ashamed.

The avoidance crept in gradually. First it was avoiding the street where the mugging happened, then the entire neighbourhood after dark, then going out at all became something Amir had to steel themselves for. Their partner, Jordan, would suggest dinner out or a walk through the park on a Saturday afternoon, and Amir would feel a familiar tightness in their chest, a cascade of reasons why it was not safe, why staying in was better. Jordan tried to be patient, but patience eroded over months. By the second year, Jordan had stopped asking. Amir realized one evening that they had not left the apartment except for work in six weeks, and even work required an elaborate mental preparation—the same route, the same times, the same scanning of every shadow. At home, the vigilance was worse. Amir had come to believe that safety was an illusion, that the mugging proved you could never truly know what was coming. Even inside, locked doors and windows checked twice, Amir felt the need to position themselves in rooms where they could see the entrance, to listen for sounds in the hallway, to check behind them when moving through the apartment. Jordan had learned not to come up behind Amir without announcing themselves first; the startle response was too violent. When Jordan would reach out to touch Amir's shoulder in the kitchen, Amir's entire body would jolt, heart racing, breath catching—a reaction that left them both shaken and reinforced Amir's conviction that danger lurked in the smallest, most ordinary moments.

What frightened Amir most was the loss of themselves. They could remember being happy, being confident, being someone who trusted the world enough to move through it freely. That person felt like a character from someone else's life. The constant vigilance had become so normal that Amir could no longer distinguish between caution and paranoia, between reasonable wariness and the exhausting conviction that danger was always one moment away. Three months ago, Jordan gave Amir an ultimatum—not cruel, but clear: get help or they could not stay. Amir realized they had become someone Jordan could no longer reach, and more terrifyingly, someone Amir themselves no longer recognized. It was that recognition, finally, that brought Amir to the clinic—not the veterinary one, but this one, to sit across from a therapist and try, once again, to find the words for what happened and what it had stolen. At twenty-six, Amir still had time to reclaim something of the person they had been, but the longer they waited, the more that possibility seemed to slip away like the September light on that street three years ago.

When the typhoon hit the coastal city where Minh had been visiting relatives, he was 22 and had never before felt the world turn so quickly from ordinary to unrecognizable. He remembered the pressure in the air first, then the noise—metal roofing tearing away, glass breaking somewhere nearby, people shouting over one another in a language that suddenly sounded thin against the wind. He had been inside a low concrete house with extended family when floodwater began forcing its way under the door. In the crush of bodies trying to move furniture, grab bags, and get older relatives upward, he strained his neck lifting and turning in tight spaces, and he still remembered the sharp pain that shot up the side of it. What stayed with him most oddly was the taste in his mouth: muddy water, dust, and something metallic he had swallowed while coughing. Even now, he said, the whole thing could feel so extreme that it was hard to believe it had really happened to him, as if he were describing a disaster film he had once watched rather than his own life.

In the weeks after he returned to the U.S., Minh tried to resume work as a UX designer, telling himself that because he was physically safe and back at his apartment, the worst should have been over. Instead, pieces of the experience arrived in disjointed ways. At times he was flooded with the same terror and helplessness he had felt in that house without seeing any clear picture at all; the emotion came first, complete and immediate, as though his body knew before his mind did. On other days he would be caught by the vivid taste again, so exact that he found himself checking his mouth or spitting into the sink. The unreality of the memory unsettled him almost as much as the intensity. If something that catastrophic could happen and still feel unreal afterward, he found himself questioning his own place in the world, as though he had crossed into a life other people could not understand.

That sense of being apart deepened in ordinary settings. When his neck stiffened after hours at his desk, or when he woke feeling vaguely feverish and physically off, he would be pulled back toward the storm. Sitting in the open-plan office, trying to review wireframes while rubbing at the base of his neck, he would suddenly taste the muddy water again or feel a wave of panic with no image attached. On days when coworkers chatted casually about travel, weather, or family plans, he felt cut off from them, convinced they inhabited a safer reality than he did. He had come to believe that people were not what they seemed: they looked dependable and ordinary until a crisis exposed how fragile everything really was. The more his body reminded him of the disaster, the more set apart he felt, and the more he withdrew into the conviction that he no longer belonged anywhere—not fully at work, not with friends, and not even with family who had not been there.

Over the following months, those beliefs began shaping what he noticed. Because he felt isolated and wary of others, trauma-related news clips, storm warnings, and even conversations about disasters landed on him with unusual force; he scanned for them and could not let them pass as background. If someone in the office mentioned extreme weather affecting a region overseas, he felt his body tense before he had fully registered the words. He was certain other people could not really grasp what danger looked like, and that certainty made reminders stand out everywhere. Once triggered, the memory returned in the same fractured form—sometimes the metallic taste, sometimes the full emotional blast without a picture—and each return seemed to confirm his view that he had been altered in a way that separated him from everyone around him.

The loop tightened further because the memories themselves made his world feel less trustworthy. When the emotional intensity hit out of nowhere, or when the taste came back with such precision, Minh took it as evidence that the disaster was still lodged just beneath the surface of ordinary life. If his own mind could pull him back so completely, he reasoned, then safety was thinner than other people believed. That left him more watchful for bodily changes and trauma-related cues, and a simple stiff neck at his workstation or a day of feeling physically unwell could set off another round. By the time he sought help, he was still managing to work, but much more narrowly than before, taking sick days when his body felt wrong and avoiding office conversations that might drift toward storms or travel. What finally brought him in was the fear that this estrangement was becoming permanent—that he would go on feeling unmoored from other people and suspicious of the ordinary world—and a quieter hope that if someone could help him make the experience feel real in a way he could bear, he might find a place for himself again.

John, a 71-year-old man of Oceania descent, has been working as a cashier at a small grocery store for over two decades. His life took an unexpected and harrowing turn one evening when he witnessed a violent armed robbery that left his coworker injured. Since then, John's daily routine has become punctuated by intrusive memories and flashbacks of the event. John still remembers the sound of shattering glass, the sight of the masked robber brandishing a gun, and the cries for help from his colleague. The trauma continues to haunt him even now, months after the incident. He often wakes up in the middle of the night with an elevated heart rate and drenched in sweat, reliving the chaos he witnessed that evening. His wife is concerned about the changes she has noticed—John becomes distant, loses focus easily, and avoids crowded places. At work, John's once reliable routine has become increasingly difficult to maintain. He often feels jumpy, especially when a customer approaches him too quickly or loudly. A few days after the robbery, he even started avoiding handling cash because it reminds him of that fateful evening. His colleagues have noticed his anxiety and the way he seems to be on edge all the time. John tries to distract himself with activities like fishing and spending time with his grandchildren but finds these once enjoyable pastimes no longer provide the same level of comfort or relief. When he goes fishing, the sound of water splashing can unexpectedly trigger a memory of the glass shattering during the robbery. He sometimes becomes so preoccupied by thoughts of that night that he finds himself unable to focus on conversations with his family members. His wife has also observed how John’s relationships have suffered. He no longer participates in their usual weekend dinners with friends and family, citing an overwhelming sense of unease in crowded settings. Even at home, he tends to isolate himself more often than before. His wife worries about the toll this trauma is taking on his mental health and their marriage. John has been experiencing a heightened state of alertness, constantly looking over his shoulder or feeling like something bad could happen at any moment. This hypervigilance makes it difficult for him to relax, even when he’s at home with his family. He gets startled easily by unexpected noises or movements, which can be distressing for both John and his wife. Despite these challenges, John is determined to find ways to cope. He sometimes writes in a journal about his feelings and thoughts related to the traumatic event, hoping that putting them into words might help him process what he experienced. However, even this form of expression feels challenging at times because the memories are so vivid and distressing. John’s work as a cashier has also been affected by the trauma. The routine interactions with customers have become sources of anxiety, and he finds himself second-guessing his every move and decision on the job. He is aware that his performance has slipped somewhat, but he feels too overwhelmed to address this openly with his manager or coworkers. As John navigates through each day, the fear and discomfort of the past continue to linger, affecting nearly all aspects of his life. His story illustrates how witnessing a traumatic event can have profound and lasting impacts on an individual's mental health and daily functioning.

Aisha, at 42, carries a quiet weariness that seems etched into her posture. Her eyes, though often downcast, hold a depth of experience that hints at a life lived through unimaginable hardship. She sits across from you, hands clasped tightly in her lap, often picking at a loose thread on her factory uniform. The story she slowly unfolds is one of survival, but also of a relentless haunting.

Her memories begin sharply with the day they came for her. It was in her home country, a place she rarely speaks of now, even to herself. One evening, men burst into her small house. The terror of that moment, the suddenness, the feeling of being utterly powerless, remains vivid. She was blindfolded, her hands bound, and shoved into a vehicle. The journey was a blur of fear and the rough jostling of the truck. Then came the dark room, the cold concrete floor, the smell of damp and something metallic she couldn't quite place. Days, or perhaps weeks—time became meaningless—were spent in isolation, punctuated by interrogations, beatings, and the constant threat of worse. She remembers the cold water, the deprivation of food, the searing pain, and the absolute certainty that she would die there. The worst, she confides, was not just the physical pain, but the systematic dismantling of her dignity, the feeling of being reduced to nothing. She learned to dissociate, to float above her body, watching the events as if they were happening to someone else. This detachment, she now realizes, never truly left her.

Eventually, she was released, or perhaps escaped – the details of her exit are still fragmented and painful for her to recall. She made her way to this new country, a refugee seeking safety. The initial relief was profound, but short-lived. The trauma followed her like a shadow. She tried to build a new life, marrying a man who had also fled his country, but the unspoken burdens eventually became too heavy. The marriage dissolved after five years, leaving her feeling even more isolated. She rarely talks about her past, even with her ex-husband, fearing judgment or simply not wanting to burden anyone.

Now, she works at a plastics manufacturing plant. The factory floor is a symphony of industrial noise: the constant hum of machinery, the rhythmic thud of presses, the high-pitched whine of conveyor belts. For Aisha, these sounds are a constant barrage of triggers. A sudden clang can send her heart racing, instantly transporting her back to the sound of a cell door slamming shut or the sharp crack of a whip. She flinches, her body tensing, and her colleagues sometimes glance at her, but she offers a quick, tight smile, pretending it was nothing. Her job requires focus, operating a machine that molds plastic components, a repetitive task that allows her mind to drift – often to places she doesn't want to go. She sees flashes of the dark room, feels the cold floor, smells the metallic odor. When this happens, her hands tremble, and she struggles to maintain precision, sometimes making mistakes that earn her a stern look from her supervisor.

Sleep offers no true escape. Most nights, she awakens in a cold sweat, gasping, her heart pounding from vivid nightmares. She's back in that room, helpless, unable to move or scream. These nights leave her exhausted, making concentration at work even harder. During the day, she's hypervigilant, constantly scanning her surroundings, even in the safety of her apartment. Every shadow, every unexpected sound, sends a jolt of fear through her. She avoids the busy breakroom at the factory, preferring to eat her lunch alone in a quiet corner, staring blankly ahead, feeling detached from the chatter and laughter of her co-workers. She feels like an outsider, unable to connect, convinced that no one could ever understand what she's been through.

Aisha rarely experiences joy anymore. The simple pleasures others talk about – a good meal, a funny movie, a walk in the park – feel distant, almost alien. She feels a pervasive numbness, as if a part of her soul was extinguished in that dark room. Sometimes, a wave of intense anger washes over her, an inexplicable rage directed at nothing in particular, leaving her feeling ashamed and confused. She often blames herself, wondering if she could have done something differently, if she somehow brought this upon herself. The future feels bleak, a continuation of this lonely, vigilant existence. She just wants to feel safe, truly safe, but the past is a relentless presence, always just beneath the surface.

It was a Tuesday evening in late October when Marco’s life fractured. He was a parole officer, fourteen years into the job, and he’d been called to a routine home check on a client in a South Side housing project. The client’s file was clean, the visit was supposed to take ten minutes. But when Marco stepped into the hallway, three plainclothes officers from a joint task force mistook him for the subject of a separate warrant. He was shoved face-first into the cinderblock wall, his arms wrenched behind his back hard enough that his right shoulder popped. One officer knelt on his neck while another screamed at him. Marco kept saying, “I’m a parole officer, I’m a parole officer,” but his badge had fallen out of his pocket and they wouldn’t listen. It took seven minutes for a supervisor to arrive and call them off. Seven minutes of his own colleagues—people who wore the same city badge he did—pressing him into the floor while he gasped for air. He was never formally apologized to. The department offered a brief internal memo. Nothing changed.

In the weeks that followed, Marco found he could only remember the event in jagged pieces—the cold of the floor, the weight on his spine, but not the face of the officer who’d knelt on him. The memory felt like a photograph torn in half; he knew the outline of what happened, but the details kept slipping away. When he tried to tell his wife, the story came out flat and distant, as if he were describing something that had happened to someone else. He found himself pushing the memory away before it could fully surface, stopping himself mid-thought because the injustice of it burned too hot. What happened to me was deeply unfair, he would think, and nothing has been done about it. The institution that should have protected me let me down. That sense of betrayal—by officers he would have once called brothers—lodged in his chest like a splinter.

The betrayal began to color everything. At work, when a parolee showed up late or lied about a drug test, Marco felt a flash of rage that was out of proportion. People misbehaving, he realized, now felt personal—a violation of an unwritten contract, the same kind of contract the officers had broken. Even ordinary stress at the office—a backlogged file, a missed deadline—triggered the same tightness in his throat. And the most potent trigger was his own body: when his heart started racing, whether from coffee or a brisk walk, he would freeze, convinced he was about to be attacked again. That pounding in his chest became a warning bell he couldn’t ignore.

He began scanning his surroundings constantly. Walking into the parole office each morning, he checked every corner, every open door, every person who stood too still. Unusual silence—the kind that fell over a hallway between conversations—made him certain something dangerous was about to happen. He startled when a coworker tapped his shoulder from behind, and the startle response itself made him feel ashamed and exposed, which only deepened his anger at the system that had turned him into this. The threat he felt was not abstract; it lived in the quiet spaces, in the weight of his own heartbeat, in every misbehaving client who reminded him that rules could be broken by anyone, including the people who were supposed to enforce them.

The cycle tightened over months. Each time Marco felt a trigger—a racing heart, a silence, a client’s lie—his mind jumped straight to the injustice of what had happened. That injustice, in turn, made the memory harder to hold onto; he would try to recall the exact moment the officer’s knee pressed into his neck, and the image would dissolve into a blur of anger and shame. The incomplete picture left him vigilant, scanning for the parts of the story he could not retrieve, and that vigilance made every silence feel like a trap. He started avoiding the South Side entirely, taking longer routes to work, and he stopped attending the department’s annual law enforcement appreciation dinner. His wife noticed he was quieter at home, that he flinched when she came up behind him in the kitchen. He told her it was nothing.

What finally brought Marco to a therapist’s office was a Tuesday morning in the parole office, when a new client—a young man with a clean record and a nervous smile—sat down across from him. The client was polite, cooperative, everything Marco should have welcomed. But the man’s stillness reminded Marco of the hallway before the officers grabbed him. Marco’s heart began to pound. He excused himself, walked to the bathroom, and stood with his hands on the sink, trying to breathe. He was terrified that he was going to lose his job. He was terrified that he had become someone who could not tell the difference between a threat and a routine Tuesday. And he was most afraid that the institution that had betrayed him had also broken something in him that could not be fixed.

Amara had learned to map danger by the temperature of the air. During those months held in a windowless room, the damp chill of early winter seeped through the concrete, matching a coldness that now lived in her chest. She remembered a hand resting too heavily on her shoulder, a voice using a name that sounded like hers to draw her eyes up. The weather that followed mirrored that exact gray, wind-driven rain, and Amara began standing by her kitchen window, watching the same slanted light while her pulse hammered before her mind could name the threat. The memory did not arrive as a story; it sat in her chest as something vast and unbelievable, as though it had happened to a woman who shared her face but not her life. When she tried to hold the details, a sharp, chemical smell rose in her throat, anchoring the fear in her lungs. Over the months, the house became a threshold requiring constant patrolling. Amara lay awake with her back to the door, her ear tuned to the hallway for a faint scrape of a hinge that never arrived. Ordinary noises—the clatter of a coffee mug, the hiss of the factory’s press machine, the crack of a delivery door—sent her shoulders locking and her heart leaping. Her body reacted to potential danger before she had time to think, mirroring the alarms that fired alongside her startle response to sounds that barely register for others. To navigate the factory floor where coworkers moved shoulder to shoulder, she started covering her face in thick layers of foundation. She stopped wearing the dark jumpsuits she once favored, convinced that similar cuts would invite the same crushing closeness. Instead, she kept her mind occupied with production quotas, humming playlists, or counting bolt alignments. When the workday ended, the silence rushed in, and she found herself scrolling or reorganizing shelves to avoid the quiet. Amara’s hands, once steady enough to calibrate machinery, now trembled when she reached for tools. She held the belief that she could no longer trust her own body, alongside the conviction that the world was a dangerous place. She watched coworkers and felt the familiar tightening in her chest, certain that strangers waited in the periphery, ready to close the distance. The world had narrowed into a series of potential encroachments. She stopped answering calls from old friends, fearing voices that might mimic the cadence of her captors. Her marriage fractured under the weight of her distance. After the divorce, she lived alone, yet the emptiness of the apartment felt more dangerous than the noise she had avoided. She held these appraisals alongside the constant monitoring of drafts, shadows, and weather shifts that carried the ghost of that cold room. By the time she stepped into the clinic, Amara had worn a path through her own life. She believed her body was a traitor, that the world could not be trusted, and that the woman who used to work the line without looking over her shoulder was gone. What frightened her most was the realization that she could no longer step outside without scanning the sky for that same gray wind, or walk into a store without pressing herself against the wall. She hoped to find a way to let her body rest, to recognize when a name was just a name and a cloud was only weather, and to reclaim the hands that felt like strangers. She was afraid of the day the distraction finally failed, of the silence catching up with her, but she knew she could not keep bracing for a storm that had already passed.

Sam is a 26-year-old non-binary veterinarian who lives with their partner in a small apartment near the animal hospital where they work. Six months ago, after a late emergency surgery, Sam walked home through the residential streets as they always had. A figure stepped out from behind a parked van, pressed something hard against their ribs, and demanded their bag. Sam remembers the smell of cheap cologne and sweat, the sound of keys jangling as the man shoved them hard against a fence before running off. The physical injuries were minor—bruises, a scraped palm—but what stayed was the cologne. It was unfamiliar, sharp, and now, without warning, it can reappear anywhere. In the exam room when a client leans close. In the hallway when a colleague walks past wearing a similar scent. Sometimes the smell comes out of nowhere, when there is no trigger Sam can identify, and the whole moment snaps back: the cold pressure, the helplessness, the certainty of being hurt.

Sam used to be a person who laughed easily, who looked forward to weekends with their partner, who felt comfortable walking into the clinic each morning. That person feels unreachable now. What frightens Sam most is the feeling that they can no longer trust their own mind. But almost as unsettling is a quieter, darker thought that has taken root: *No one else can really help me.* That night, after the mugging, Sam had stumbled to a nearby convenience store, but the clerk had barely looked up from his phone, and nobody on the street had called out or come to check on them. Since then, Sam has come to believe that other people—even those who care—cannot truly be relied on to step in when it counts. Their partner is kind, yes, but Sam finds themselves thinking, *What would they actually do if someone broke in?* They can't shake the sense that, ultimately, Sam is alone with the fear. When they try to tell their partner what happened, the story comes out in fragments—they lose the thread halfway through, forget what came next, and end up staring at the floor while the silence stretches. Sometimes Sam finds themselves thinking, *It wasn’t that bad. Maybe I’m overreacting. Maybe I imagined the whole thing.* That thought brings a moment of relief, but it never lasts. The smell returns. The fear returns. And Sam is left feeling hollow and confused—and more certain than ever that no one else can truly understand or protect them.

At work, Sam has become someone their colleagues describe as jumpy. They scan the parking lot before unlocking the door in the morning. They check over their shoulder every few steps when walking to the supply shed. At home, they can’t sit with their back to the door. Even in the apartment, surrounded by their partner’s presence, Sam feels a low hum of alert—a readiness to respond to the wrong sound, a footstep in the hallway, a key in the lock. They have become meticulously careful: they lock the door twice, avoid going out after dark, and ask their partner to pick up groceries or run errands. Driving has become their only safe way to move through the city, because walking means vulnerability and the constant need to check behind them. Yet even when their partner agrees to help, Sam feels a knot of resentment and distrust—*They're only doing this because I asked, not because they truly get it.* The thought is unfair, Sam knows, but it lingers.

The avoidance has consequences. Sam’s partner has begun to seem tired of being asked to handle every evening trip. There is a quiet strain between them, a sense of distance that Sam does not know how to bridge. At the clinic, Sam had an incident last month with a client who became angry over a billing error. The client raised his voice, stepped closer to the counter. Sam felt their whole posture change—they started nodding, apologizing, offering discounts, agreeing to anything. Later, they could not explain why they had given in so easily. The fawning felt automatic, a survival script that had taken over. That evening, at home, Sam sat in the dark and could not stop their hands from trembling. They did not tell their partner. What was the point? *They wouldn't know what to say, and I'd just feel stupid.*

The breaking point came two weeks ago. During a routine procedure on a dog with a bleeding wound, Sam’s nose caught a faint trace of a cologne on the owner’s clothing. The smell was not the same, but similar enough. Sam froze mid-movement, the memory flooding back, the room dissolving. They excused themselves, handed the surgery to a colleague, and locked themselves in the bathroom, unable to speak or explain. Their supervisor expressed concern and recommended a leave of absence. Sam is now sitting in a therapist’s office for the first time, terrified that they will never feel normal again. They are not sure what they hope for—maybe just that someone will listen without judging, that they will learn to trust their own mind again. But deep down, Sam doesn't believe that any single person can truly keep them safe. They are here, though, because the alternative—continuing alone—feels even worse.
